name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,824

entries.clue: Get cold feet crossing lake in total darkness (8)

indicatorNotes.crossing: A road crossing a field cuts straight through the middle of it, so the letter named next lands inside the words before it.

blocks.note: getting cold feet about a promise is backing out of it
L is lake on a map and in a gazetteer

annotation.surface: Losing your nerve halfway across a lake in the pitch dark.
annotation.walkthrough: The cold feet are nothing to do with cold water: to get cold feet is to pull out of something promised. 'Crossing' reads as the swim and is the instruction that one piece goes inside another.
annotation.definitionFit: A blackout is a total loss of light, a whole street or a whole stage going dark at once.

entries.clue: Don't disturb new yeast, say (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The 'say' owns up to yeast being one raising agent among several — sourdough starter is another — rather than a straight synonym.

blocks.note: told not to disturb something, you leave it alone
n. is the short form of new

annotation.surface: A note asking that the fresh yeast be left alone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Don't disturb' reads as the sign on a hotel door and is a plain verb meaning let alone. Leaven is what bakers call the agent that lifts a dough, so the definition is the trade's word rather than the shopper's.
annotation.definitionFit: A leaven is any agent that makes dough rise, and yeast is the one every baker reaches for first.

entries.clue: Group of weirdos one's holding at court (9)

indicatorNotes.holding: Whatever you are holding is inside your grip, so the letters just named close round the piece that follows.

blocks.note: a cult is the group whose devotion looks weird from outside it
one has shortens to I've, with one written as the letter I
the word itself, dropped in whole

annotation.surface: A gang of oddballs that somebody is keeping hold of in court.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Court' is the verb and not the building: to court someone is to work on them for their favour. 'One's' is one has, which the grid spells I've.
annotation.definitionFit: To cultivate a useful contact is to court them, tending the friendship for what it may one day bring.

entries.clue: Egg supplier to diversify, starting with duck (5)

indicatorNotes.starting with: What a word starts with stands at its front, so the letter named after this goes before everything else.

blocks.note: in cricket a duck is a score of nought, and the grid writes that 0 as the letter it looks like
to vary your stock is to diversify it

annotation.surface: Advice to a poultry farmer to branch out, beginning with ducks.
annotation.walkthrough: A batsman out without scoring in cricket is out for a duck, and that nought is the letter wanted here. 'Egg supplier' sounds like the farm gate and names an organ.
annotation.definitionFit: An ovary is the organ in which a female's eggs are made and from which they are released, so every egg comes out of one.

entries.clue: Opera the Parisian makes smaller but with similar parts (2,5)

blocks.note: Puccini's Tosca, the opera of Scarpia and the leap from the battlements
the Parisian says the in French, and this is the masculine form of it

annotation.surface: An opera that a Parisian shrinks while keeping all its proportions.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The Parisian' is the crossword's standing request for a French word, here the article itself. 'Parts' sounds like the roles an opera is cast with and means the pieces a model is built from; 'similar' is the geometer's word for the same shape at a different size.
annotation.definitionFit: A drawing or a model made to scale is reduced by the same ratio in every direction, so its parts keep the proportions of the real thing.

entries.clue: Likelihood Charlie Chan switched back from Chinese? (6)

indicatorNotes.switched: Two names switched have changed places, so the second of them is written down first.
indicatorNotes.back from: The back of a word is its final letter, and that is all this takes from the word after it.

blocks.note: the detective's surname, written out whole
Charlie is C in the radio alphabet, the first name cut to its initial
the hindmost letter of CHINESE

annotation.surface: The odds on the detective Charlie Chan having swapped back out of being Chinese.
annotation.walkthrough: Charlie Chan is the Honolulu detective of the 1930s film series, which is what lets the whole surface stay on one man. Only the first name comes down to an initial; the surname keeps all four of its letters and then goes in front.
annotation.definitionFit: A chance is how likely a thing is — 'what chance is there of rain?' asks exactly that.

entries.clue: Evita, say, Argentinian revolutionary guards escort (9)

indicatorNotes.say: Say admits that the person named is only an instance, so what is wanted is the wider description she fits.
indicatorNotes.guards: A guard stands round what he is protecting, so the letters named first close on either side of the ones named next.

blocks.note: Che Guevara, the Argentine doctor who became Castro's commander, is the crossword's revolutionary
Evita is Eva Peron, Argentina's first lady, and she is one of the Perons rather than the only one

annotation.surface: An Argentinian revolutionary standing guard over somebody's escort.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wordplay are Argentine and both sit in the surface, which is why nothing in the sentence looks out of place. Evita was the wife of President Juan Peron, and 'say' warns that she is one Peron of two.
annotation.definitionFit: A chaperone is the older companion who goes along to keep a young person respectable, which is to escort them.

entries.clue: Bail screwed on stump, possibly as form of defence (5)

indicatorNotes.screwed: A screwed-up piece of paper is crumpled out of all shape, and these letters come out of it in a new order.
indicatorNotes.on: In a down entry what sits on something rests above it, so this piece takes the squares over the letter named next.
indicatorNotes.possibly: Possibly allows the thing named to be one example of what is meant, so a single upright stick stands in for the letter it resembles.

blocks.note: the four letters of BAIL, reordered
a stump is one of the three upright sticks of a cricket wicket, and a lone upright is the shape of this letter

annotation.surface: A cricket bail screwed onto a stump as a way of defending the wicket.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is all cricket: the bail is the little bar balanced on top of the stumps, and a batsman really does defend his wicket. The stump earns its letter by shape alone, which is what 'possibly' owns up to.
annotation.definitionFit: An alibi is the plea that you were somewhere else at the time, which is one recognised form of defence in a court.

entries.clue: Keep prisoner in during day (8)

indicatorNotes.during: What happens during the day happens inside it, so the letters named here sit within the word that follows.

blocks.note: a con is a convict
Tue is the diary's short way of writing Tuesday
the word itself, taken as it stands

annotation.surface: Holding a prisoner inside for the day.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Keep' has to be heard as keep going rather than keep hold of, which is the sense the prisoner in the surface is pushing. The day is a particular one, abbreviated as a diary abbreviates it.
annotation.definitionFit: To keep at something is to continue with it — keep walking, keep talking — so the verb keep carries the sense of not stopping.

entries.clue: Stop barking to wiry Alsatian (7,7)

indicatorNotes.barking: Barking is British slang for raving mad, after the east London suburb, and letters gone mad will not keep the order they were given in.

blocks.note: fourteen letters to rearrange, the full width of the entry

annotation.surface: Telling a wiry Alsatian to stop barking.
annotation.walkthrough: The dog is the trap: 'Alsatian' looks like the thing being shouted at and is eight letters of the fodder. Only the first word of the clue is the definition, and it is a noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A stop on a line is where the train pulls in and lets people off, so every station on a railway is one of its stops.

entries.clue: Hilarity seeing Strauss's name on his pants today, inside out (6)

indicatorNotes.inside out: A bag turned inside out has everything in the middle of it tipped away, leaving only what was at the two ends.

blocks.clueFragment: seeing Strauss's name on his pants
blocks.note: Levi Strauss stitched his own first name onto the jeans he made, and it is on the label still
TODAY with everything between its first letter and its last taken away

annotation.surface: Laughing at the name Strauss has printed on the trousers he is wearing today.
annotation.walkthrough: Strauss is Levi, the Bavarian who riveted the first jeans, not the waltz composer. Pants are trousers to him and underwear to a British reader, which is where the surface gets its snigger.
annotation.definitionFit: Levity is treating a thing as a laughing matter, so a room full of levity is a room full of hilarity.

entries.clue: A sort of tripe provided stimulation for diner (8)

indicatorNotes.sort of: To sort a thing is to put it into an arrangement other than the one it arrived in, which is what happens to the letters beside this.

blocks.note: the article, taken as it stands
the five letters of TRIPE, reordered
provided that you come and if you come say the same thing

annotation.surface: A kind of offal that got the diner's appetite going.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Provided' looks like the waiter's verb and is the conjunction if. Tripe is the stomach lining of a cow, a dish that flatters nobody, and the word for nonsense besides.
annotation.definitionFit: An aperitif is the small drink taken before a meal to sharpen the appetite, so it is exactly what stimulates a diner.

entries.clue: One and a half chaps & I make cheese (8)

indicatorNotes.a half: Counting one of them as a half means taking half of the word and no more, its first two letters of four.

blocks.note: the chaps are being counted, and one whole chap is a man
half of CHAP is the first two of its four letters
the ego is the I, Freud's Latin for the self

annotation.surface: A head count of the chaps present — one and a half of them, plus me.
annotation.walkthrough: Manchego is the sheep's-milk cheese of La Mancha, which is also where 13 down's knight rode from, so the Spanish joke runs through the puzzle. The I of the clue is the ego of psychoanalysis.
annotation.definitionFit: Manchego is the firm sheep's-milk cheese of La Mancha, sold under that name on every Spanish deli counter.

entries.clue: Writer never acts in play (9)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition names the trade and the answer is one particular practitioner of it, the usual licence for a proper noun.

indicatorNotes.in play: A ball in play is one still moving about the field, and letters in play move about just as freely.

blocks.note: nine letters to rearrange

annotation.surface: A writer who never takes a part in a play.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word after the first is either fodder or instruction, which is what makes the sentence about a shy playwright read so smoothly. Cervantes wrote Don Quixote, the book European novelists have been answering ever since.
annotation.definitionFit: Cervantes wrote Don Quixote, along with plays, poems and a shelf of novellas, so writer is his trade.

entries.clue: Swallow something slimy on lettuce? (4)

blocks.note: the noun, not the verb: a single gulp of a strong drink
the shell-less garden pest that leaves a trail across the salad bed

annotation.surface: Being told to swallow the slimy thing that was sitting on the lettuce.
annotation.walkthrough: The two halves run together into one queasy instruction, which is the whole trick. Nothing is assembled anywhere in this clue: both halves are meaning.
annotation.definitionFit: A slug of whisky is one swallow of it, and the slug of the vegetable patch is the slimy creature chewing through the lettuces.

entries.clue: Empty supermarket as well as till, for challenge (5,2,2)

indicatorNotes.Empty: An emptied box has had its contents taken out of it, so the word this applies to keeps only the letters at its two ends.

blocks.note: SUPERMARKET with everything between its first letter and its last cleared out
two things listed as well as each other are joined by this word
wait till six and wait up to six name the same moment

annotation.surface: Robbers clearing out a supermarket and its till too.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Till' is the shop's cash drawer in the surface and the preposition meaning until in the wordplay. The definition is a verb, the thing you do to a bully rather than a thing you set someone.
annotation.definitionFit: To stand up to a bully is to challenge them rather than give way, meeting the thing head on.

entries.clue: Ill-treated donkey in race died (8)

indicatorNotes.in: A donkey in a race is inside it, so the letters named next go between the letters of the word named first.

blocks.note: to hare off down the road is to race off
an ass is a donkey
d. is died, as written in a family tree

annotation.surface: A badly treated donkey that died during a race.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Race' looks like the event the donkey was entered for and is the verb, the one a hare does. The single letter at the end is the abbreviation carved on gravestones.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody harassed has been pestered and chivvied until they are worn down, which is ill-treatment of a wearing kind.

entries.clue: You hear greeting very well (4)

indicatorNotes.You hear: What you hear is a sound and not a spelling, so the word named is to be taken by ear.

blocks.note: a greeting called out across a street is a hail, and the sound is written the other way here

annotation.surface: Somebody catching a greeting perfectly clearly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Very well' reads as how clearly the greeting came through and means in good health. Hail as a greeting survives in hail-fellow-well-met and in the older carols.
annotation.definitionFit: Hale means sound in body — hale and hearty — so a person who is hale is a person who is very well.

entries.clue: Tree, said lecturer after Spooner (3,5)

indicatorNotes.after Spooner: The Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of two neighbouring words, and doing a thing after him is doing it his way.

blocks.note: said on its own is sed, and it takes the r that the next word lets go of
a reader is a senior university lecturer in Britain, and with the s-sound of the word before at its front it is spelt this way

annotation.surface: A lecturer naming a tree straight after Spooner has had his turn.
annotation.walkthrough: Say the two plain words aloud and trade the noises at their fronts: the s travels forwards, the r travels back, and the vowels shift a little as they go. Reader is a rank, not a hobby.
annotation.definitionFit: The red cedar is a timber tree, the western red cedar of North America, whose scented wood lines wardrobes and clads sheds.

entries.clue: Make jewels set with diamonds for amusement (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The dodgems are always spoken of in the plural, one attraction made of many cars, so a singular definition names the ride as a whole.

indicatorNotes.set with: A ring set with a stone has the stone fixed into the middle of it, so the letter named last goes inside what came before.

blocks.note: to do a meal and to make one come to the same thing
gems are jewels, cut and polished stones
D is diamonds on a bridge scoresheet

annotation.surface: A jeweller making jewels set with diamonds, purely for the fun of it.
annotation.walkthrough: Diamonds are the card suit here, which is why the jewellery of the surface can keep them company so quietly. 'Make' is the plainest verb in the language and hands over its two most useful letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The dodgems are the fairground's bumper cars, ridden for the fun of crashing into your friends, which is an amusement in the funfair's sense of the word.

entries.clue: Artist back in cells after spitting curry (6)

indicatorNotes.back in: The back of a word is the end of it, so only the final letter of the word named here is taken.
indicatorNotes.after: In a down entry what comes after something is written below it, so the letters named first sit under the piece named next.

blocks.note: spitting with rage and mad with rage describe one temper
RA is a Royal Academician, the crossword's standing artist
the hindmost letter of CELLS

annotation.surface: An artist back behind bars after spitting his curry out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spitting' is the temper, as in spitting with rage, and not what the artist does to his dinner. Madras is the old name of the south Indian city now called Chennai.
annotation.definitionFit: A madras is the medium-hot curry every British Indian restaurant lists, named after the city it is supposed to come from.

entries.clue: Crazy world left Alan Alda short changed (2-2,4)

indicatorNotes.short: Somebody cut short stops before the end, so the name beside this gives up its last letter.
indicatorNotes.changed: Money changed comes back in a different form, and these letters come back in a different order.

blocks.note: L is left, as marked on a pair of gloves
the actor's full name with its last letter dropped, seven letters to work with

annotation.surface: A mad world that left the actor Alan Alda short-changed.
annotation.walkthrough: Short-changed is one grievance in the surface and two separate instructions in the wordplay, a word each. Alan Alda is the American actor who played Hawkeye in MASH.
annotation.definitionFit: La-la land is the dreamy state of somebody out of touch with reality, a whole world of their own making that is not quite sane.

entries.clue: A right horror (5)

blocks.note: the article, taken as it stands
in law this is the creditor's right to keep your property until a debt is paid

annotation.surface: Somebody written off as an absolute horror.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A right horror' is how a British speaker says somebody is dreadful, and the wordplay takes the middle word literally, as a right in law.
annotation.definitionFit: An alien is the invading creature of the horror film, the monster from elsewhere, so it is named here by the fright it gives.

entries.clue: Trial or settlement? (6)

blocks.note: the word itself, taken as it stands
the deal two sides strike is the settlement they reach

annotation.surface: A lawyer asking whether the case goes to court or settles.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Or' is not offering a choice at all: it is two of the letters, sitting in plain sight. The definition wants trial in the sense of a hard time, not the hearing the surface conjures.
annotation.definitionFit: A trial is any experience that tests your endurance — the journey was a trial — which is what an ordeal is.

entries.clue: Time doctor reversed conclusion (5)

indicatorNotes.reversed: A thing reversed faces back the way it came, so the letters gathered before this word are read from the far end.

blocks.note: the age of steam is the time of steam
the MO is the medical officer, the doctor attached to a unit

annotation.surface: A doctor of time who overturned the conclusion.
annotation.walkthrough: Omega ends the Greek alphabet, which is why it stands for the end of anything at all — alpha and omega, the first and the last. The doctor is the army's, not the surgery's.
annotation.definitionFit: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, so it is used for the end of a series and the conclusion of any business.

entries.clue: Channel Islanders' capital isn't safe, jest banks (5,5,4)

annotation.definitionNote: The town is Guernsey's capital rather than the whole archipelago's — Jersey keeps its own at St Helier — so the definition credits the islanders collectively with one island's seat.

indicatorNotes.banks: A river's banks run along either side of it, so the word named here splits and takes a side each.

blocks.note: said in sport and said in jest both mean said for the fun of it
ain't is the informal way of saying it
a peter is a safe in old criminal slang, the thing a peterman blows open

annotation.surface: Talk of offshore money that isn't safe, with the banks treating it as a joke.
annotation.walkthrough: The Channel Islands' offshore banking is what 'capital' and 'banks' are there to suggest, and neither word is doing that job. St Peter Port is Guernsey's harbour town, climbing the hill above the marina.
annotation.definitionFit: St Peter Port is Guernsey's harbour town and the seat of its government, the capital of the largest of the Channel Islands.

entries.clue: Who's 13's hero? Someone really good-looking (6)

blocks.note: a question of the form who's that? is answered a … is, which puts an A at the front and an IS at the back
the writer at 13 down sent a Spanish don tilting at windmills

annotation.surface: A quiz question about 13's hero, answered with a remark about his looks.
annotation.walkthrough: Answer the clue's own question and you have spelt it: a don is. Cervantes's knight is Don Quixote, and it is the Spanish title rather than the name that the grid wants.
annotation.definitionFit: An Adonis is a strikingly handsome man, named for the youth Aphrodite fell for, and the word is used of anyone really good-looking.

entries.clue: Fish are sighted almost jumping ashore (8)

indicatorNotes.almost: Almost means all of it but the end, so the word this applies to stops one letter short.
indicatorNotes.jumping: A fish jumping is out of the water and out of place, and these letters land in an order of their own.

blocks.note: to sight a thing is to see it, and the word is cut one letter short of the end
the six letters of ASHORE, reordered

annotation.surface: Fish spotted almost leaping out onto the beach.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a shoal in the shallows and the answer is the one fish that never leaps anywhere. 'Are sighted' is asking for the plain verb see, which the next word then docks.
annotation.definitionFit: The seahorse is a true fish, with gills and fins like any other, for all that it swims upright and wears a horse's head.
